title: The source texts
lead:
This is the evidence behind the report, in the words it was first written in. Each passage is given in Greek, Latin or Syriac, with the edition it comes from, an English rendering, and what scholars on different sides make of it. If a scholar's reading of a text seems too neat, you can check it against the text itself here.

You don't need to read Greek or Latin to use these pages. The English sits right under each original, and the notes say where a word is disputed and why.

parts.title: Origen in his own words
parts.lead: Most of what Origen wrote is lost, and much of the rest survives only in Latin translations made a century and a half after his death. These files show what he says, and where the text itself is the problem.

parts.title: The condemnations
parts.lead: Every time Origen or his ideas were condemned, from his own bishop in the 230s to the councils of the seventh and eighth centuries, in the order they happened.

parts.title: The wider argument
parts.lead: The texts both sides lean on when they argue about the condemnations: the monk whose ideas the sixth century condemned, the Bible verses in dispute, and other early Christian writers who hoped for, or ruled out, an end to punishment.

files.title: On First Principles
files.blurb: The book the condemnations quote most, and the argument over whose version of it to trust.
files.lead: *On First Principles* (in Greek *Peri Archon*) is the book Origen's critics always went back to. The whole of it survives only in Rufinus's Latin of 398, which Rufinus admits he smoothed over. Hostile readers, Jerome and Justinian among them, quoted other versions. Which text you trust goes a long way toward deciding what Origen taught.

files.title: Origen's other works
files.blurb: What he says about punishment and the end in works that survive in Greek.
files.lead: Some of Origen's works survive in his own Greek, so they don't carry the doubts that hang over Rufinus's Latin. These are the passages scholars on both sides cite most often when they ask what he believed about punishment and the end of all things.

files.title: The first censure, c. 231
files.blurb: Why his own bishop turned on him, and Origen's answer.
files.lead: The first condemnation came from Origen's own bishop, Demetrius of Alexandria, about 231. What we know of it comes from later writers, chiefly Eusebius and Photius, and from a letter of Origen's own that survives in two Latin versions that don't agree.

files.title: The controversy around 400
files.blurb: Epiphanius, Jerome, Theophilus and Pope Anastasius: what they condemned and why.
files.lead: A century and a half after his death, Origen became the center of a bitter quarrel. Epiphanius of Salamis attacked him, Jerome turned against him, and in 400 Theophilus of Alexandria and Pope Anastasius condemned his books. Most of these texts survive in Jerome's Latin.

files.title: Justinian's edict of 543
files.blurb: The emperor's ten anathemas, the plainest text against universal restoration.
files.lead: In 543 the emperor Justinian wrote a long letter against Origen to Menas, the patriarch of Constantinople, and ended it with ten anathemas. (An anathema is a solemn curse that cuts someone off from the church.) The ninth is the plainest condemnation of universal restoration anywhere in the record.

files.title: The fifteen anathemas of 553
files.blurb: The anathemas against an Origenist system, and the ancient reports of them.
files.lead: In 553 the bishops gathered at Constantinople signed fifteen anathemas against Origenist teaching. They aren't in the council's official record, and most historians now think they were signed just before it opened. This file gives them in Greek, with the ancient reports of what the council did.

files.title: Was Origen's name added later?
files.blurb: Every place a council names Origen, and how secure the name is in each.
files.lead: Some scholars have argued that Origen's name was slipped into the condemnations after the fact. The argument is almost entirely about one list, the eleventh anathema of the council of 553. This file goes through every council and document that names him and asks how secure the name is in each.

files.title: Later councils and church statements
files.blurb: The councils of 649, 680 and 787, the Synodikon of Orthodoxy, and modern statements.
files.lead: Whatever happened in 553, later councils took it that Origen had been condemned and said so. This file follows that through the seventh and eighth centuries and into the statements churches make today.

files.title: Evagrius and the sixth-century Origenists
files.blurb: The monk whose ideas the anathemas of 553 most closely match.
files.lead: Evagrius of Pontus, a monk who died in 399, built on Origen's ideas. In 1958 Antoine Guillaumont published the full Syriac text of Evagrius's *Kephalaia Gnostica*, and showed that the anathemas of 553 follow it closely. That finding changed the whole debate about what 553 condemned.

files.title: The Bible verses in dispute, and Gregory of Nyssa
files.blurb: "God all in all", "eternal punishment", and the universalism of a saint never condemned.
files.lead: Both sides argue from the same few verses of the New Testament. And both have to account for Gregory of Nyssa, who taught that evil will one day be gone entirely and who has always been venerated as a saint.

files.title: Other early writers for and against an end to punishment
files.blurb: Basil, Augustine, Gregory Nazianzen, Maximus the Confessor, Isaac of Nineveh and the Antiochenes.
files.lead: Origen was not the only early Christian to hope that punishment might end, and not every writer who rejected the hope did so in the same way. These are the other voices both sides call on.

how_to_read:
## How to read these pages

**How far each text was checked.** Each passage carries a letter. **V** means the text was compared with an edition, or a scan of one. **S** means it was checked against a scholar's quotation of it, because no edition could be reached online. **R** means it wasn't checked. Each scholar's reading carries the same kind of note: read in their own words, taken from a reliable report, or a standard attribution not yet checked.

**Translations.** Older translations whose copyright has run out, such as the nineteenth-century *Ante-Nicene Fathers* and *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers* (ANF and NPNF), are quoted and named. Everywhere else the English is our own close translation, and the standard published translation is named so you can compare.

**Editions.** A critical edition is a scholar's text built from the surviving manuscripts. The abbreviations you'll meet most are: **ACO**, the acts of the councils (Schwartz, Straub, Riedinger); **CCSL** and **CCSG**, the Corpus Christianorum Latin and Greek series; **CSEL**, the Vienna Corpus of Latin church writers; **GCS**, the Berlin series of Greek Christian writers; **GNO**, the Leiden edition of Gregory of Nyssa; **PG** and **PL**, Migne's nineteenth-century Greek and Latin patrologies; **PO**, Patrologia Orientalis; **SC**, Sources Chrétiennes. Many of the texts here were checked against the open digital editions of the First1KGreek and Open Greek and Latin projects.
